newsitem.title: USA: Wet weather bogs down late U.S. wheat planting.
newsitem.headline: Wet weather bogs down late U.S. wheat planting.

text.p: The soybean harvest is nearly complete in the eastern Corn Belt, but heavy rains this week could prevent some farmers from planting double-crop soft red winter wheat, agronomists and producers there said.
"Anybody that double-cropped this year isn't going to plant wheat," said Jim Beuerlein, extension agronomist with Ohio State University. "I think they'll be some acres abandoned."

Because approximately 50 percent of the soybean crop was planted in Ohio in June rather than May, as many as 250,000 of Ohio's estimated 1.25 million acres devoted to soft red winter wheat will not be planted this year, Beuerlein said.
Ohio and Indiana received heavy rains overnight Thursday, and private forecasters were calling for more precipitation this weekend in northern areas of those states.

Parts of Indiana received up to 3.0 inches of rain on Thursday, and most of Ohio saw heavy rain as well, growers said. Because the ground was already saturated, the additional rain will leave fields unworkable until next week.
"They're worrying more about wheat," one Ohio-based cash merchant said. "We've gone so late on the beans, who knows what will happen if you plant wheat now."
Winter wheat sowing dates were already delayed this season by the late planting of the soybean crop, so this week's rainy weather is seen pushing some soybean harvest dates closer to Thanksgiving.

"We're already a month behind the ideal planting date for this area, so some of them (farmers) may choose not to plant winter wheat at all," said Chuck Mansfield, a Purdue University extension agronomist based in southwestern Indiana.
The drawn-out soybean harvest as well as the poor performance and health of the 1995 soft red winter wheat crop has cut the number of acres devoted to wheat, agronomists said.
"Late planting has clobbered them (producers) two years in a row," Beuerlein said.
Mansfield said soft red winter wheat acreage in southwest Indiana could be down as much as 50 percent in some cases.

However, the latest crop progress reports from state agricultural statistics services in Illinois, Indiana and Ohio showed that most of the soft red winter wheat crop in those states had been planted.

In Indiana, 88 percent of the winter wheat acreage had been seeded by the week ended November 3, versus 97 percent last year. In Ohio, 91 percent of the crop had been seeded versus 100 percent last year while Illinois SRW wheat was 90 percent seeded, slightly behind 96 percent last year and 92 percent average.
